title: What Makes a Good TOK Exhibition Prompt Choice?
summary: Learn what makes a strong TOK exhibition prompt choice, how to test possible objects, avoid weak links, and plan effectively during the IB fall term.
body_markdown:
A good TOK exhibition prompt choice gives you access to **three specific real-world objects** , distinct lines of analysis, and repeated opportunities to address the prompt's exact wording. The best prompt is not necessarily the most philosophical. It is the one you can explore clearly through objects whose contexts you understand and whose inclusion you can justify.


This matters during the **IB TOK fall term** , when many students move from broad interests to a workable prompt and object set. Your school's internal deadlines take priority, but September to November is a useful period for testing combinations before drafting.


### Understand the official TOK exhibition task


The[IB overview of Theory of Knowledge](https://ibo.org/programmes/diploma-programme/curriculum/dp-core/theory-of-knowledge/) explains that TOK is assessed through an exhibition and a 1,600-word essay. The exhibition is the internally assessed component, worth **33% of the final TOK result** , and is externally moderated.


You must choose **one of the 35 prescribed IA prompts** and explore it through **three objects or images of objects** . The accompanying commentary has a maximum of **950 words in total** , not 950 words per object. The objects should demonstrate how TOK manifests in the world around us.


Copy the prompt exactly from the official list supplied by your teacher. You cannot rewrite it, combine prompts, or use a different prompt for each object. The[RevisionDojo guide to TOK exhibition prompts](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/tok-exhibition-prompts-b4a14cd7) can help you compare their focus, but your school's current materials remain authoritative.


### What makes a good TOK exhibition prompt choice?


A strong choice passes four tests: **interpretive clarity, object availability, analytical depth, and variety** . You should understand what the prompt asks, have suitable objects available, and be able to develop three related but non-repetitive arguments.


### You understand the controlling terms


Identify the words that shape the question. In “What counts as good evidence for a claim?”, the important terms include **counts** , **good evidence** , and **claim** . The prompt asks how standards of adequate evidence are established, not simply for three examples of evidence.


Write a one-sentence interpretation in your planning notes. If you cannot explain the knowledge problem plainly, connecting objects to it precisely will be difficult. Your interpretation supports the analysis but does not replace the prescribed wording.


### You can identify specific objects


A workable prompt should generate several particular objects in identifiable contexts, not generic categories.


- “A scientific article” is generic.
- “The printed 2024 journal article my biology class used to evaluate a disputed health claim” is specific.
- “Social media” is a broad topic.
- “A screenshot of a corrected post published by a named organization on a known date” is contextualized.


Specificity matters because an object's origin, audience, purpose, and history provide evidence for analysis. The[official IB activity using AI-generated content as a TOK object](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/tok-activity-using-ai-generated-content-as-a-tok-object-en.pdf) shows that a digital item can work when it is identifiable and placed in context.


### The objects make different contributions


Three objects should not produce three versions of the same argument. One might support a direct response to the prompt, another might reveal a limitation, and the third could introduce a different perspective or standard.


For a prompt about experts, one object could demonstrate successful reliance on specialist authority. A second could reveal expert disagreement, while a third examines how audiences decide which expert deserves trust. Every object addresses the same prompt, but each has a separate analytical role.


### The prompt supports analysis


A strong pairing allows discussion of **evidence, justification, interpretation, authority, values, certainty, methods, or responsibility** . Ask what the object shows about how knowledge is produced, accepted, communicated, or challenged. If your answer only summarizes the object, the connection needs refinement.


### Use a prompt feasibility test


Shortlist **three or four prompts** , then test each before committing. A planning table prevents you from choosing a prompt merely because it sounds impressive.


Test Question Warning sign


Interpretation Can I explain the exact knowledge problem? I only repeat the prompt.


Object access Can I identify four specific objects? I have topics, not objects.


Context Do I know where, when, and why each was used? The object is an anonymous image.


Analysis Can each object support a knowledge claim? I can only describe it.


Variety Do three objects offer different insights? All three prove the same point.


Evidence Can I verify contextual claims? My reasoning depends on assumptions.


Score each prompt from **0-2** on every test. This is not an IB mark, but it exposes hidden weaknesses. A less dramatic prompt may be better if it produces clearer contexts and stronger analysis.


### A worked prompt-choice example


Consider “How can we distinguish between knowledge, belief and opinion?” A student might test it with a school laboratory report, a family letter expressing a conviction, and a specific editorial from a local debate.


These objects could examine methodological justification, personal belief, and public opinion. However, the student must avoid claiming that belief is automatically irrational, opinion is always uninformed, or a scientific report provides certainty. The tensions between the categories create the analysis.


### Common prompt-selection mistakes


- **Choosing the prompt before testing objects:** Sketch the context, claim, and contribution of at least three objects. The[RevisionDojo object-selection guide](https://www.revisiondojo.com/blog/selecting-the-right-objects-for-your-tok-exhibition) provides useful diagnostic questions.
- **Using objects as symbols:** A lock does not automatically explore ownership of knowledge. The object's real use must reveal something about the prompt.
- **Treating a topic as a prompt:** Technology, culture, and bias are interests, not prescribed IA prompts. Begin with the exact official question.
- **Assuming objects must be sentimental:** Personal engagement may come from studying, using, encountering, or questioning an object. Public documents and digital objects can also work.
- **Choosing the supposedly easiest prompt:** Popular prompts can still produce vague claims. Assessment depends on the quality of your links and justification.


### A September-to-November TOK plan


Adapt this sequence to your teacher's deadline.


- **September:** Read all prompts, annotate their controlling words, and shortlist three or four. Use the[RevisionDojo TOK resource hub](https://www.revisiondojo.com/ib/ib-theory-of-knowledge-tok) to clarify central concepts.
- **Early October:** Generate four or five objects for each shortlisted prompt. Record each object's identity, context, possible claim, and source requirements.
- **Late October:** Choose the strongest combination. Explain every link aloud and remove objects that require forced reasoning.
- **November:** Confirm the plan with your teacher, collect images, verify contextual facts, and outline each object's contribution.


Do not wait until drafting to decide what each object does. The commentary is easier to control when every object already has a clear intellectual function.


### Academic integrity and final checks


Your final selection, reasoning, and writing must remain your own. The[IB academic integrity policy](https://www.ibo.org/globalassets/new-structure/programmes/shared-resources/pdfs/academic-integrity-policy-en.pdf) requires transparency when AI-generated material is included in assessed work. Jojo AI can ask diagnostic questions, but it should not write your submitted commentary; follow your school's AI policy.


Before committing, confirm that you have one accurately copied prompt, three contextualized objects, three distinct analytical contributions, evidence for factual claims, and a plan that fits the **950-word maximum** . You can consult[TOK exhibition examples](https://www.revisiondojo.com/coursework-exemplars/tok-exhibition) and the[RevisionDojo TOK Exhibition Grader](https://www.revisiondojo.com/grader/rubric/tok-exhibition) , but never copy their language or object combinations.


### Conclusion


A good TOK exhibition prompt choice has practical analytical potential. Choose a prompt you understand, test it against specific objects, and ensure the final three offer different insights anchored to the exact question. RevisionDojo's TOK Study Notes, Jojo AI, examples, and TOK Exhibition Grader can support this process alongside feedback from your teacher.
